XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Since the United Kingdom was formed, 65 countries have become independent. How many of those have asked to come back? And what is unique about Wales that you think Wales is incapable of running its own affairs?
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: Ers ffurfio'r Deyrnas Unedig, mae 65 o wledydd wedi dod yn annibynnol. Faint o'r rheini sydd wedi gofyn am ddod yn ôl? A beth sy'n unigryw am Gymru i wneud i chi feddwl na all Cymru redeg ei materion ei hun?

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl Reform UK: Cymru a'r Deyrnas Unedig
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Reform UK Debate: Wales and the United Kingdom
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Let's get back to the questions, which you didn't answer, by the way, okay. So, what currency would we use? No answer. Would Welsh citizens retain the right, the automatic right that they currently have today, to live, work and study elsewhere in the UK? They can't tell us. Would Welsh businesses retain unfettered access to our most important market in England, Scotland and Northern Ireland? They have absolutely no idea. Would the so-called party of Wales seek to rejoin the European Union that was rejected—[Interruption.]—that was rejected by the people of Wales? And I know—[Interruption.] And I know it's an inconvenient truth for you to hear, but the people of Wales voted to leave the EU. Who would be our head of state? Who would be our head of state? They have no answer whatsoever. I know they want to abolish the monarchy, but who's going to be the president? No answer. Would taxes rise, spending fall, or borrowing go through the roof because you can't afford to pay for the unaffordable promises that you have made to the people of Wales because of that huge fiscal gap that would cost every single taxpayer, by the way, in the whole of our country, about £14,000 each and every single year? That's the reality. Would Wales have its own armed forces? Would you join NATO? Would you join NATO?

You cannot answer these things. And they're not technicalities; these concern people's jobs, savings, mortgages, pensions, national security and our clout on the international stage. I'm not prepared to take that risk. I firmly believe that Wales is better off in the United Kingdom and that the United Kingdom is better off with Wales right at the very centre of everything that it does. I'm proud to be a member of the Welsh Conservatives and the Conservative and Unionist Party.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Gadewch inni droi'n ôl at y cwestiynau, na wnaethoch chi eu hateb, gyda llaw. Felly, pa arian fyddem ni'n ei ddefnyddio? Dim ateb. A fyddai dinasyddion Cymru yn cadw'r hawl, yr hawl awtomatig sydd ganddynt heddiw ar hyn o bryd, i fyw, gweithio ac astudio mewn mannau eraill yn y DU? Ni allant ddweud wrthym. A fyddai busnesau Cymru yn cadw mynediad dirwystr i'n marchnad bwysicaf yn Lloegr, yr Alban a Gogledd Iwerddon? Nid oes unrhyw syniad ganddynt. A fyddai plaid pobl Cymru fel y'i gelwir yn ceisio ailymuno â'r Undeb Ewropeaidd a wrthodwyd—[Torri ar draws.]—a wrthodwyd gan bobl Cymru? Ac rwy'n gwybod—[Torri ar draws.] Ac rwy'n gwybod ei fod yn wirionedd anghyfleus i chi ei glywed, ond pleidleisiodd pobl Cymru dros adael yr UE. Pwy fyddai ein pennaeth gwladwriaeth? Pwy fyddai ein pennaeth gwladwriaeth? Nid oes ganddynt ateb o gwbl. Rwy'n gwybod eu bod eisiau diddymu'r frenhiniaeth, ond pwy fydd yr arlywydd? Dim ateb. A fyddai trethi'n codi, gwariant yn gostwng, neu fenthyca'n mynd trwy'r to am na allwch fforddio talu am yr addewidion anfforddiadwy rydych chi wedi'u gwneud i bobl Cymru oherwydd y bwlch cyllidol enfawr a fyddai'n costio tua £14,000 y flwyddyn i bob trethdalwr, gyda llaw, yn ein gwlad gyfan? Dyna'r realiti. A fyddai gan Gymru ei lluoedd arfog ei hun? A fyddech chi'n ymuno â NATO? A fyddech chi'n ymuno â NATO?

Ni allwch ateb y pethau hyn. Ac nid manylion technegol ydynt; mae'r rhain yn ymwneud â swyddi pobl, cynilion, morgeisi, pensiynau, diogelwch cenedlaethol a'n dylanwad ar y llwyfan rhyngwladol. Nid wyf i'n barod i gymryd y risg honno. Rwy'n credu'n gryf fod Cymru'n well yn y Deyrnas Unedig a bod y Deyrnas Unedig yn well gyda Chymru yng nghanol popeth y mae'n ei wneud. Rwy'n falch o fod yn aelod o'r Ceidwadwyr Cymreig a'r Blaid Geidwadol ac Unoliaethol.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch, Lywydd. Mae'n amlwg, wrth edrych ar y cynnig a'r gwelliannau sydd wedi'u gosod y prynhawn yma, fod dwy agwedd wahanol iawn i'w cael am ddyfodol Cymru yn y Siambr hon.

Gwnaf i droi'n gyntaf at gynnig gwreiddiol Reform. Dwi'n siŵr y bydd yr eironi'n glir i bawb, wrth i blaid sydd yn gwneud chwarae mawr ar bwysigrwydd rhyddid barn geisio cyfyngu ar hawl bobl Cymru i gynnal trafodaeth adeiladol dros ddyfodol ein gwlad. Trafodaeth ar eu termau nhw yn unig ydy ffordd Reform. Wrth i'r twf am gefnogaeth dros newid cyfansoddiad yng Nghymru barhau, mae ei strategaeth am amddiffyn statws cwo y Deyrnas Unedig a thaflu amheuaeth dros fanteision datganoli yn groes i beth mae mwyafrif o bobl Cymru yn dymuno ei weld.

A dyma droi at welliant Llafur. Ie, geiriau cynnes am ddatganoli a'i holl fanteision ar bapur, ond fel y gwelsom dros y ddwy flynedd o'u partneriaeth mewn grym bob ochr i'r M4, dydyn nhw'n golygu dim mewn realiti. Er bod y cyfarwyddyd wedi dod erbyn hyn i fod yn fwy cefnogol o ddatganoli gan eu pennaeth newydd yn Downing Street, maen nhw'n ei chael hi'n anodd i hyd yn oed argyhoeddi eu Haelodau eu hunain yn San Steffan am yr angen am fwy o ddatganoli.

Yn yr etholiad, fe wnaeth pobl Cymru ei gwneud hi'n glir eu bod nhw'n dymuno mwy o bwerau dros eu dyfodol eu hunain, ond fe ddaru nhw hefyd ei gwneud hi'n berffaith glir nad ydyn nhw'n credu bod Llafur o ddifrif dros weithredu'r dyheadau hynny, sydd yn dod â fi at welliant Plaid Cymru. Yn syml, rydym ni'n coelio mai pobl Cymru a phobl Cymru yn unig ddylai fod â'r hawl i benderfynu dros ddyfodol ein hunain. Nid breuddwydion cyfansoddiadol ydy'r rheini, ond hawl sydd yn cael ei roi i bron i bob gwlad ddemocrataidd arall ar draws y byd. Wrth osod ein gwelliant heddiw, rydym yn ceisio datgloi'r sgwrs am ddyfodol ein gwlad. Mae'r pleidiau eraill yn benderfynol o'i chadw dan glo. Ai dyma'r gorau all pethau fod i Gymru?

Yn ystod yr haf, es i draw i Slofenia, gwlad sydd efo miliwn yn llai o bobl na Chymru, gwlad a fynnodd ei hannibyniaeth er gwaethaf amgylchiadau economaidd a chymdeithasol heriol. Ond erbyn hyn, mae hi'n wlad sydd wedi gwneud i'w heconomi dyfu mwy na saith gwaith dros y blynyddoedd diwethaf, yn wlad sydd wedi manteisio ar ei haelodaeth o'r Undeb Ewropeaidd, ac yn wlad sydd wedi adeiladu ei heconomi ar y sectorau ynni a thwristiaeth. Mae'r gymhariaeth â Chymru yn hynny o beth yn glir.

Yn bersonol, dydw i ddim yn credu bod San Steffan yn gweithio i'n cenedl, ond pobl Cymru ddylai fod â'r grym i gael dweud eu dweud ar hynny, nid Whitehall. I gloi, Lywydd, dywedodd Matthew Rhys wythnos diwethaf,
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Thank you, Llywydd. It's clear, in looking at the motion and the amendments tabled this afternoon, that there are two very different views on the future of Wales in this Chamber.

I will turn first of all to Reform's original motion. I'm sure that the irony will be palpable to all, as a party that makes great play of the importance of freedom of opinion seeks to limit the right of the people of Wales to have a constructive discussion on the future of our nation. A discussion on their own terms, that's all Reform are interested in. As the growth in support for constitutional change continues, their strategy of protecting the status quo of the UK and casting doubt on the benefits of devolution is contrary to the view of the majority of the people of Wales.

And let's turn now to the Labour amendment. Yes, warm words about devolution and all its benefits on paper, but as we saw over the two years of their partnership in power at both ends of the M4, they mean nothing in practice. Although the direction has come now to be more supportive of devolution from their new head in Downing Street, they are finding it difficult to even convince their own Members in Westminster of the need for further devolution.

In the election, the people of Wales made it clear that they wanted more powers over their own future, but they also made it perfectly clear that they don't believe that Labour is serious about acting on those aspirations, which brings me to the Plaid Cymru amendment. Simply, we believe that the people of Wales and the people of Wales alone should have the right to determine their own future. Those aren't constitutional dreams, but a fundamental right that is afforded to almost every other democratic nation across the world. In tabling our amendment today, we are seeking to unlock the conversation about the future of our nation. The other parties are determined to keep it under lock and key. Is this the best things can be for Wales?

During the summer, I went over to Slovenia, a nation with a million fewer people than Wales, a nation that insisted on its independence despite a challenging economic and social environment. But now it's a nation that has caused its economy to grow more than sevenfold over recent years, a nation that has benefited from its membership of the European Union, and a nation that has built its economy on the energy and tourism sectors. The comparison with Wales in that regard is quite clear.

Personally, I don't believe that Westminster is working for our nation, but the people of Wales should have the power to have their say on that issue, not Whitehall. To conclude, Llywydd, Matthew Rhys said last week,

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Reform UK Debate: Wales and the United Kingdom
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
The United Kingdom is the greatest nation in the history of the world. We gave parliamentary democracy, common law and the industrial age—I'm glad you're laughing, it's not funny. We defeated Napoleon. We abolished the slave trade—sorry to disappoint you. We stood against Hitler in 1940 when the rest of Europe had fallen.

And at every one of those moments, Wales was there. Wales has been at the centre of British history for generations. In 1485, Henry Tudor, a Welshman born in Pembroke castle, landed near Milford Haven. He marched through Wales, gathering men to his banner, the Red Dragon, and he took the crown at Bosworth. His granddaughter Queen Elizabeth I began the British empire, which was such a force for good in the world. Sorry, Carrie. Welsh minds then went on to shape the modern world. William Grove from Swansea invented the fuel cell in 1842, a technology the world is still using today.

In Mumbles, a constituency I used to represent as a councillor, we pioneered the world's first passenger railway. Merthyr became the largest ironworks on earth. In Swansea, we smelted so much of the world's copper that we were famously called Copperopolis, for your information. Welsh steam coal fuelled the Royal Navy, and the first cheque for £1 million was signed at the Coal Exchange in Cardiff—[Interruption.] Welsh iron made the—no, we haven't got enough time, thank you, and this is important—railway of the empire. Welsh coal powered the fleet that protected them.

When Britain went to war, Wales answered. At Rorke's Drift, in 1879, Wales's 24 Regiment of Foot held off thousands and won 11 Victoria Crosses in a single action. A Welsh Prime Minister, David Lloyd George, led us to victory in the great war. The Welsh Guards were formed in 1915 and have served this country in every major conflict since. In February 1941, Swansea endured three nights of the Blitz and our town did not break. In 1982, Welsh Guards gave their lives in the Falklands war, defending British people and British soil. That is our history.

Welsh blood, Welsh industry and Welsh genius are written into every chapter of the British story. So, when I look at the politics of Wales today, I see people in positions of power who are working to tear that story apart. Plaid claimed during the election that independence wouldn't be an issue, but now the mask has slipped. Their true colours have now been shown, thanks to their meeting with Sinn Féin, the political wing of the IRA. There are Members in this Chamber who want to break up the United Kingdom. They want to walk away from the shared resources that fund our schools, our hospitals, our pensions and our armed forces. They want to take Wales out of the most successful union the world has ever seen, and they can't even tell the people of Wales the basics of what currency we'd use or how we would pay our way.

For nearly 30 years of devolution, Cardiff Bay has been obsessed with the constitution—more politicians, more powers, more bureaucracy and more red tape. And through all of it, Wales has remained at the bottom of the UK for income, employment and for our health and education outcomes. Westminster Governments of every colour carry their share of blame. They have spent years apologising for Britain instead of celebrating us. They have allowed our history to be rewritten as a list of crimes. They have forced mass immigration and its terrible consequences on our people. They have let energy prices in the land of coal and steam rise to some of the highest in the developed world, and they have watched Welsh steel furnaces go cold. The people of Wales and the United Kingdom deserve better than a political class that is embarrassed by their own country. They want to abandon the values that made us great in the first place.

This month, September, marks my eighteenth anniversary as an officer in the Royal Air Force Air Cadets, an organisation whose ethos represents the true spirit of this country. I am proud to be Welsh. I am proud to be British. Two things, as Darren said, that should never be in conflict. I want my children—my two boys—to learn about Henry Tudor, Rorke's Drift and the Falklands war. I want them to know that Wales helped to shape the world that we live in today, the bonds and the sacrifices we have shared, and I want Wales to remain where she belongs, at the very heart and soul of the United Kingdom.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Y Deyrnas Unedig yw'r genedl wychaf yn hanes y byd. Fe wnaethom roi democratiaeth seneddol, cyfraith gyffredin a'r oes ddiwydiannol—rwy'n falch eich bod chi'n chwerthin, nid yw'n ddoniol. Fe wnaethom drechu Napoleon. Fe wnaethom ddiddymu'r fasnach gaethweision—mae'n ddrwg gennyf eich siomi. Fe wnaethom sefyll yn erbyn Hitler ym 1940 pan oedd gweddill Ewrop wedi cwympo.

Ac ym mhob un o'r rheini, roedd Cymru yno. Mae Cymru wedi bod yng nghanol hanes Prydain ers cenedlaethau. Ym 1485, fe wnaeth Harri Tudur, Cymro a anwyd yng nghastell Penfro, lanio ger Aberdaugleddau. Gorymdeithiodd trwy Gymru, gan gasglu dynion at ei faner, y Ddraig Goch, a chipiodd y goron yn Bosworth. Dechreuodd ei wyres, y Frenhines Elizabeth I, yr ymerodraeth Brydeinig, a oedd yn gymaint o rym er lles yn y byd. Mae'n ddrwg gennyf, Carrie. Yna aeth meddyliau Cymreig yn eu blaenau i siapio'r byd modern. Dyfeisiodd William Grove o Abertawe y gell danwydd ym 1842, technoleg y mae'r byd yn dal i'w defnyddio heddiw.

Yn y Mwmbwls, etholaeth yr oeddwn i'n arfer ei chynrychioli fel cynghorydd, fe wnaethom arloesi gyda rheilffordd gyntaf y byd i deithwyr. Merthyr oedd y gwaith haearn mwyaf ar y ddaear. Yn Abertawe, fe wnaethom doddi cymaint o gopr y byd nes inni gael ein galw'n Copperopolis, er gwybodaeth i chi. Glo stêm Cymreig oedd yn tanio'r Llynges Frenhinol, a llofnodwyd y siec gyntaf am £1 filiwn yn y Gyfnewidfa Lo yng Nghaerdydd—[Torri ar draws.] Haearn Cymru—na, nid oes gennym ddigon o amser, diolch, ac mae hyn yn bwysig—a luniodd reilffyrdd yr ymerodraeth. Glo Cymru a bwerodd y fflyd a'i hamddiffynnai.

Pan aeth Prydain i ryfel, fe atebodd Cymru. Yn Rorke's Drift, ym 1879, cadwodd Catrawd 24 Troedfilwyr Cymru filoedd draw ac ennill 11 Croes Fictoria mewn un ymgyrch. Cawsom ein harwain i fuddugoliaeth yn y rhyfel mawr gan Brif Weinidog o Gymru, David Lloyd George. Ffurfiwyd y Gwarchodlu Cymreig ym 1915 ac maent wedi gwasanaethu'r wlad hon ym mhob gwrthdaro mawr ers hynny. Ym mis Chwefror 1941, dioddefodd Abertawe dair noson o'r Blitz ac ni dorrodd ein tref ni. Ym 1982, rhoddodd y Gwarchodlu Cymreig eu bywydau yn rhyfel y Falklands, gan amddiffyn Prydeinwyr a thir Prydeinig. Dyna ein hanes.

Mae gwaed Cymreig, diwydiant Cymreig ac athrylith Gymreig wedi'u hysgrifennu ym mhob pennod o'r stori Brydeinig. Felly, pan edrychaf ar wleidyddiaeth Cymru heddiw, rwy'n gweld pobl mewn swyddi pwerus sy'n gweithio i chwalu'r stori honno. Honnodd Plaid Cymru yn ystod yr etholiad na fyddai annibyniaeth yn broblem, ond nawr mae'r mwgwd wedi llithro. Mae eu gwir liwiau bellach wedi'u dangos, diolch i'w cyfarfod â Sinn Féin, adain wleidyddol yr IRA. Mae yna Aelodau yn y Siambr hon sydd eisiau chwalu'r Deyrnas Unedig. Maent eisiau cerdded i ffwrdd oddi wrth yr adnoddau a rennir sy'n ariannu ein hysgolion, ein hysbytai, ein pensiynau a'n lluoedd arfog. Maent eisiau tynnu Cymru allan o'r undeb mwyaf llwyddiannus y mae'r byd wedi'i weld erioed, ac ni allant ddweud wrth bobl Cymru beth yw'r pethau sylfaenol hyd yn oed ynglŷn â pha arian y byddem yn ei ddefnyddio neu sut y byddem yn talu ein ffordd.

Am bron i 30 mlynedd o ddatganoli, mae Bae Caerdydd wedi bod ag obsesiwn gyda'r cyfansoddiad—mwy o wleidyddion, mwy o bwerau a mwy o fiwrocratiaeth. A thrwy hynny i gyd, mae Cymru wedi aros ar waelod y DU o ran incwm, cyflogaeth a'n canlyniadau iechyd ac addysg. Mae Llywodraethau San Steffan o bob lliw yn ysgwyddo eu cyfran o'r bai. Maent wedi treulio blynyddoedd yn ymddiheuro dros Brydain yn hytrach na'i dathlu. Maent wedi caniatáu i'n hanes gael ei ailysgrifennu fel rhestr o droseddau. Maent wedi gorfodi mewnfudo torfol a'i ganlyniadau ofnadwy ar ein pobl. Maent wedi gadael i brisiau ynni yng ngwlad glo a stêm godi i rai o'r rhai uchaf yn y byd datblygedig, ac maent wedi gwylio ffwrneisi dur Cymru yn oeri. Mae pobl Cymru a'r Deyrnas Unedig yn haeddu gwell na dosbarth gwleidyddol sydd ag embaras ynghylch eu gwlad eu hunain. Maent eisiau rhoi'r gorau i'r gwerthoedd a'n gwnaeth ni'n wych yn y lle cyntaf.

Y mis hwn, mis Medi, mae deunaw mlynedd ers imi ddechrau fel swyddog gyda Chadetiaid Awyr yr Awyrlu Brenhinol, sefydliad y mae ei ethos yn cynrychioli gwir ysbryd y wlad hon. Rwy'n falch o fod yn Gymraes. Rwy'n falch o fod yn Brydeinwraig. Dau beth, fel y dywedodd Darren, na ddylai wrthdaro byth. Rwyf am i fy mhlant—fy nau fab—ddysgu am Harri Tudur, Rorke's Drift a rhyfel y Falklands. Rwyf am iddynt wybod bod Cymru wedi helpu i siapio'r byd rydym yn byw ynddo heddiw, y cysylltiadau a'r aberth rydym wedi'u rhannu, ac rwyf am i Gymru aros lle mae hi'n perthyn, wrth galon ac enaid y Deyrnas Unedig.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl Reform UK: Cymru a'r Deyrnas Unedig
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Reform UK Debate: Wales and the United Kingdom
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Of course, if Wales was an independent country, it would be the one hundred and thirty seventh largest country in world, sandwiched in size between Mongolia and Uruguay. We also know that countries around the world have a GVA—a measure of the value of goods and services produced in the economy—that is lower than that of Wales: Haiti. So why, having identified that Wales is neither too small nor too poor to be independent, do I oppose independence? The primary reason is straightforward, and it rests on both Wales's tax receipts and its GVA. An independent Wales would, based upon published data, be poorer than we are now, with a combination of higher taxes and poorer public services. 

Plaid Cymru's policy is one of salami-slicing to independence, summed up by 'Devolve, devolve and devolve until there's nothing left to devolve.' Adam Price, when leader of Plaid Cymru, said,

'Plaid Cymru has a simple answer to the challenge posed by Westminster, and that is independence.'

Please ignore that Wales is financially a net beneficiary of the union. We know that because David Phillips of the Institute for Fiscal Studies has estimated that Wales is a net beneficiary of the union by between £12 billion and £15 billion a year. If Wales keeps its revenue and funds its own public spending and then makes a population-based contribution for UK-wide situations, at least understand there would be a large fiscal deficit for Wales. Also according to David Phillips of the IFS, the most recent estimates from the ONS suggest that, for public expenditure, Wales is about 10 per cent higher than across the UK as a whole. This is despite raising substantially less money. We know that, in devolved areas, Wales gets 20 per cent more than England. We know the commission chaired by Gerry Holtham said Wales needs 15 per cent more than England. That is the Barnett floor. Funding cannot fall below that level. The finance Cabinet Minister confirmed that the Holtham committee figure was correct. So, when Wales looks at fair funding, Plaid Cymru, it means we want £1 billion less.

We also know small countries don't have the economic strength to weather financial storms. For example, in Iceland, between 2008 and 2010, a catastrophic financial crash occurred. This involved the default of all three of the country's major privately owned commercial banks in late 2008, following problems in refinancing their short-term debt and a run on deposits. Relative to the size of its economy, Iceland's systematic banking collapse was the largest of any country in economic history. The crisis led to a severe recession and the mass migration of younger people. That's what happens when you play games. It's not those of us who are of retirement age or near retirement age or settled, it's the young people who are forced to leave because there's no employment for them.

I believe in devolution, but not in Welsh independence. We've had seven devolution settlements for Wales, and we're no closer to a long-term settlement than we were before the first. In the UK, we've seen different devolution settlements for Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, as well as different responsibilities devolved to London and some of the larger city regions of England. There are obvious areas that need to be held centrally within a devolved structure, such as defence, foreign affairs, national security, currency, interest rates, overseas aid, immigration, driver and car licensing, central bank and national insurance numbers. If they are not held centrally, that's called independence. Is there any of those that Plaid Cymru do not want devolved on their journey to independence? If those areas are devolved, well that is independence.

Now, should taxation change and there be UK taxes to pay for centrally funded items with all other taxes devolved and collected locally? That's what happens in America for state and national taxes. How will financial support from the wealthier to the poorer regions be organised and maintained? We do not know the direction of devolution.

Not everything needs to be devolved to Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland or the English city region at the same time. What we should have is a list of items that are available to be devolved, with each Parliament and mayoral area needing at least two thirds of its Members voting in favour for that area to be devolved. This is what happened with policing in Northern Ireland. It was devolved because two thirds of the Northern Ireland Assembly voted for it. This approach avoids big-bang devolution, where control of everything is passed on one day, while still allowing the matter to be devolved as the Parliaments are ready for them and funding is agreed. The advantage of this is that it sets an end point to the devolution journey, outside of creating new countries, and allows each to move at a pace it is comfortable with, with a common end point.

Asymmetric devolution hasn't worked in Britain. It didn't work in Spain. Other countries, like Germany and USA, have the same powers devolved. Each US state has the same powers and responsibility, no matter its size. It's the same with each German Land. But devolution in Wales does not have to end in Cardiff. Devolution in Wales is possible to be devolved to the four regions of Wales and to councils. Which powers would be better devolved to local authorities also needs to be discussed and decided.

The twentieth century is almost a one-way journey of items being taken off local authorities and then dealt with centrally. And I think, really, we want to do what is best for Wales, not what is best for our political views.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Wrth gwrs, pe bai Cymru'n wlad annibynnol, byddai yn safle 137 yn y byd o ran ei maint, rhwng Mongolia ac Uruguay. Gwyddom hefyd fod gan wledydd ledled y byd werth ychwanegol gros—mesur o werth nwyddau a gwasanaethau a gynhyrchir yn yr economi—sy'n is na gwerth Cymru: Haiti. Felly, ar ôl nodi nad yw Cymru yn rhy fach nac yn rhy dlawd i fod yn annibynnol, pam fy mod i'n gwrthwynebu annibyniaeth? Mae'r prif reswm yn syml, ac mae'n dibynnu ar dderbyniadau treth Cymru a'i gwerth ychwanegol gros. Yn seiliedig ar ddata a gyhoeddwyd, byddai Cymru annibynnol yn dlotach nag ydyw nawr, gyda chyfuniad o drethi uwch a gwasanaethau cyhoeddus tlotach.

Polisi o doriadau tameidiog sydd gan Blaid Cymru o ran annibyniaeth, wedi'i grynhoi gan 'Datganoli, datganoli a datganoli nes na fydd dim byd ar ôl i'w ddatganoli.' Dywedodd Adam Price, pan oedd yn arweinydd Plaid Cymru,

'Mae gan Blaid Cymru ateb syml i'r her sy'n wynebu San Steffan, sef annibyniaeth.'

Anwybyddwch y ffaith bod Cymru'n fuddiolwr net o'r undeb yn ariannol. Gwyddom hynny oherwydd bod David Phillips o'r Sefydliad Astudiaethau Cyllidol wedi amcangyfrif bod Cymru yn fuddiolwr net o'r undeb ar rhwng £12 biliwn a £15 biliwn y flwyddyn. Os yw Cymru'n cadw ei refeniw ac yn ariannu ei gwariant cyhoeddus ei hun ac yna'n gwneud cyfraniad ar sail poblogaeth ar gyfer sefyllfaoedd ledled y DU, o leiaf deallwch y byddai diffyg cyllidol mawr i Gymru. Hefyd, yn ôl David Phillips o'r Sefydliad Astudiaethau Cyllidol, mae'r amcangyfrifon diweddaraf gan y Swyddfa Ystadegau Gwladol yn awgrymu bod Cymru, ar gyfer gwariant cyhoeddus, tua 10 y cant yn uwch nag ar draws y DU gyfan. Mae hyn er gwaethaf codi llawer llai o arian. Gwyddom fod Cymru, mewn meysydd datganoledig, yn cael 20 y cant yn fwy na Lloegr. Gwyddom fod y comisiwn dan gadeiryddiaeth Gerry Holtham wedi dweud bod angen 15 y cant yn fwy ar Gymru na Lloegr. Llawr Barnett yw hynny. Ni all cyllid syrthio o dan y lefel honno. Cadarnhaodd y Gweinidog Cabinet dros gyllid fod ffigur pwyllgor Holtham yn gywir. Felly, pan fydd Cymru'n edrych ar gyllid teg, Blaid Cymru, mae'n golygu ein bod ni eisiau £1 biliwn yn llai.

Rydym hefyd yn gwybod nad oes gan wledydd bach gryfder economaidd i wrthsefyll stormydd ariannol. Er enghraifft, yng Ngwlad yr Iâ, rhwng 2008 a 2010, digwyddodd cwymp ariannol trychinebus. Golygodd fod pob un o dri banc masnachol mawr preifat y wlad mewn diffyg ar ddiwedd 2008, yn dilyn problemau i ailariannu eu dyled tymor byr a thynnu adneuon. O'i gymharu â maint ei heconomi, cwymp bancio systematig Gwlad yr Iâ oedd y mwyaf mewn unrhyw wlad o fewn hanes economaidd. Arweiniodd yr argyfwng at ddirwasgiad difrifol ac ymfudo torfol pobl ifanc. Dyna beth sy'n digwydd pan fyddwch chi'n chwarae gemau. Nid y rheini ohonom sydd ar oedran ymddeol neu'n agos at oedran ymddeol neu wedi setlo sy'n dioddef ond y bobl ifanc sy'n cael eu gorfodi i adael am nad oes gwaith ar eu cyfer.

Rwy'n credu mewn datganoli, ond nid mewn annibyniaeth i Gymru. Rydym wedi cael saith setliad datganoli i Gymru, ac nid ydym yn agosach at setliad hirdymor nag yr oeddem cyn y cyntaf. Yn y DU, rydym wedi gweld gwahanol setliadau datganoli ar gyfer Cymru, yr Alban a Gogledd Iwerddon, yn ogystal â gwahanol gyfrifoldebau wedi'u datganoli i Lundain a rhai o ddinas-ranbarthau mwy o faint Lloegr. Mae yna feysydd amlwg sydd angen eu cadw'n ganolog mewn strwythur datganoledig, megis amddiffyn, materion tramor, diogelwch cenedlaethol, arian cyfred, cyfraddau llog, cymorth tramor, mewnfudo, trwyddedu gyrwyr a cheir, banc canolog a rhifau yswiriant gwladol. Os na chânt eu cynnal yn ganolog, gelwir hynny'n annibyniaeth. A oes unrhyw un o'r rheini nad yw Plaid Cymru eisiau eu datganoli ar eu taith tuag at annibyniaeth? Os yw'r meysydd hynny'n cael eu datganoli, wel dyna yw annibyniaeth.

Nawr, a ddylai trethiant newid a bod trethi yn y DU i dalu am eitemau a ariennir yn ganolog gyda'r holl drethi eraill wedi'u datganoli a'u casglu'n lleol? Dyna beth sy'n digwydd yn America ar gyfer trethi gwladwriaethol a chenedlaethol. Sut y bydd cymorth ariannol gan y rhanbarthau cyfoethocach i'r rhai tlotach yn cael ei drefnu a'i gynnal? Nid ydym yn gwybod beth yw cyfeiriad datganoli.

Nid oes angen datganoli popeth i Gymru, yr Alban, Gogledd Iwerddon neu ddinas-ranbarthau Lloegr ar yr un pryd. Yr hyn y dylem ei gael yw rhestr o eitemau sydd ar gael i'w datganoli, gyda phob Senedd ac ardal faerol angen o leiaf dwy ran o dair o'i Haelodau i bleidleisio o blaid datganoli'r ardal honno. Dyma beth a ddigwyddodd gyda phlismona yng Ngogledd Iwerddon. Cafodd ei ddatganoli am fod dwy ran o dair o Gynulliad Gogledd Iwerddon wedi pleidleisio drosto. Mae'r dull hwn o weithredu yn osgoi datganoli ar amrantiad, lle mae rheolaeth ar bopeth yn cael ei basio ar un diwrnod, gan ganiatáu i'r mater gael ei ddatganoli pan fydd y Seneddau'n barod ar ei gyfer a chyllid wedi'i gytuno. Mantais hyn yw ei fod yn gosod pwynt terfyn i'r daith ddatganoli, y tu allan i greu gwledydd newydd, ac yn caniatáu i bob un symud ar gyflymder y mae'n gyfforddus ag ef, gyda phwynt terfyn cyffredin.

Nid yw datganoli anghymesur wedi gweithio ym Mhrydain. Ni weithiodd yn Sbaen. Mae gan wledydd eraill, fel yr Almaen ac UDA, yr un pwerau wedi'u datganoli. Mae gan bob talaith yn yr Unol Daleithiau yr un pwerau a chyfrifoldeb, beth bynnag yw ei maint. Mae'r un peth yn wir gyda'r Länder Almaenig. Ond nid oes rhaid i ddatganoli yng Nghymru ddod i ben yng Nghaerdydd. Mae'n bosibl datganoli yng Nghymru i bedwar rhanbarth Cymru ac i gynghorau. Mae angen trafod a phenderfynu pa bwerau fyddai'n well eu datganoli i awdurdodau lleol.

Mae'r ugeinfed ganrif bron yn daith unffordd o eitemau wedi'u tynnu o ddwylo'r awdurdodau lleol ac yna'u trin yn ganolog. Ac rwy'n credu, mewn gwirionedd, ein bod ni eisiau gwneud yr hyn sydd orau i Gymru, nid yr hyn sydd orau i'n safbwyntiau gwleidyddol.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Reform UK Debate: Wales and the United Kingdom
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch, Llywydd. Just before I speak, I just wanted to echo what somebody else has said, and I really do think the First Minister should be in the Chamber for what I think is one of the most important debates that we'll have, together with some other Cabinet Members who are missing too.

So, when we debate Wales's place in the United Kingdom, we should do so with our eyes wide open about what separation would actually involve, because this isn't just about flags, slogans or constitutional theory. It is also about people's jobs, pensions, taxes and public services.

So, let's start with the numbers. Some of these have been mentioned already, but I want to go through them again with a little bit more detail. UK public sector debt now stands at almost £3 trillion, okay? There is no agreed formula determining how much of that debt Wales would inherit if it became independent, because that would still have to be negotiated. But just to understand the scale involved, if debt were divided according to population, Wales's share would be around £136 billion. That's approximately £43,000 for every man, woman and child here in Wales, and that's before we even consider Wales's annual finances.

The latest official figures show public expenditure attributed to Wales at around £20,000 per person, whilst revenue raised is only around £13,000. That gap of more than £7,000 per person equates to another figure that was mooted earlier, which is almost £23 billion every single year. Those figures don't tell us exactly what the finances of an independent Wales would look like, and nobody can honestly claim they do, but they do demonstrate the scale of the questions that would have to be answered. Who pays for the NHS? Who pays pensions? What taxes would have to rise? What spending would have to fall? And also, what currency would be used? Nobody seems to know. Who services that debt? And what happens to the fiscal transfers that currently operate across the United Kingdom? Those aren't scare stories; they're legitimate questions involving billions of pounds of taxpayers' money.

But our United Kingdom is about far more than just a balance sheet. Look at the history, some of which has been mentioned earlier, represented by families throughout Wales. Our fathers, grandfathers and great-grandfathers served alongside men and women from England, Scotland and Northern Ireland through two world wars. Welsh regiments fought with extraordinary courage, Welsh communities endured loss and sacrifice, and families waved loved ones goodbye, never knowing whether they would return. They served as part of the armed forces of the United Kingdom, and that shared history matters.

It doesn't dictate what constitutional decisions future generations must make—those decisions belong to us—but neither should we casually dismiss the bonds forged through generations of shared sacrifice, shared endeavour and shared achievements. Those bonds continue today. People cross the Wales and England border every day to work, trade, study, receive healthcare and visit their families. Businesses operate across it, supply chains cross it, families cross it. We share armed forces, we share economic institutions, we share risks. When one part of the United Kingdom needs support, resources can move between its nations and regions.

Wales can proudly and distinctively remain Welsh, whilst remaining part of something bigger too. Our language, our culture, our communities and our national identity do not depend upon erecting a new international border. When independence is proposed, the debate must go beyond the emotional appeal of greater sovereignty. Those advocating fundamental constitutional change need credible answers about debt, the fiscal deficit, pensions, currency, trade, defence and the funding of public services. The numbers involved are simply too large and the consequences too important for anything less. I believe every single one of us in this Chamber has a responsibility to understand the history and the legacy of the United Kingdom that generations before us helped us to build, defend and pass on.

We should think very carefully before taking divisive and potentially irreversible steps without confronting all of the consequences for those who come after us. For my part, I am proud to be Welsh, I am proud to be British, and I will continue to make the case for protecting our place within the United Kingdom, not only because of the history we share, but because of the future we still have the opportunity to build together. Diolch.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Diolch, Lywydd. Cyn imi siarad, roeddwn i eisiau adleisio'r hyn y mae rhywun arall wedi'i ddweud, ac rwy'n credu y dylai'r Prif Weinidog fod yn y Siambr ar gyfer yr hyn y credaf ei bod yn un o'r dadleuon pwysicaf a gawn, ynghyd ag Aelodau Cabinet eraill sydd ar goll hefyd.

Felly, pan fyddwn yn trafod lle Cymru yn y Deyrnas Unedig, dylem wneud hynny gyda'n llygaid ar agor ynglŷn â'r hyn y byddai gwahanu yn ei olygu mewn gwirionedd, oherwydd nid baneri, sloganau neu theori gyfansoddiadol yn unig yw hyn. Mae'n ymwneud hefyd â swyddi pobl, pensiynau, trethi a gwasanaethau cyhoeddus.

Felly, gadewch inni ddechrau gyda'r ffigurau. Mae rhai o'r rhain wedi'u crybwyll eisoes, ond rwyf eisiau mynd drwyddynt eto mewn ychydig mwy o fanylder. Mae dyled sector cyhoeddus y DU bron yn £3 triliwn erbyn hyn, iawn? Nid oes fformiwla gytûn sy'n penderfynu faint o'r ddyled honno y byddai Cymru yn ei hetifeddu pe bai'n dod yn annibynnol, oherwydd byddai'n rhaid trafod hynny. Ond i ddeall ei maint, pe bai'r ddyled yn cael ei rhannu yn ôl poblogaeth, byddai cyfran Cymru oddeutu £136 biliwn. Mae hynny'n golygu oddeutu £43,000 ar gyfer pob dyn, menyw a phlentyn yma yng Nghymru, a hynny cyn inni hyd yn oed ystyried cyllid blynyddol Cymru.

Mae'r ffigurau swyddogol diweddaraf yn dangos bod gwariant cyhoeddus a briodolir i Gymru oddeutu £20,000 y pen, tra bod y refeniw a godir yn ddim ond oddeutu £13,000. Mae'r bwlch hwnnw o fwy na £7,000 y pen yn cyfateb i ffigur arall a gafodd ei wyntyllu yn gynharach, sef bron i £23 biliwn bob blwyddyn. Nid yw'r ffigurau hynny'n dweud wrthym yn union sut olwg fyddai ar gyllid Cymru annibynnol, ac ni all neb honni'n onest y gallant wneud hynny, ond maent yn dangos maint y cwestiynau y byddai'n rhaid eu hateb. Pwy sy'n talu am y GIG? Pwy sy'n talu pensiynau? Pa drethi fyddai'n rhaid eu codi? Pa wariant fyddai'n gorfod lleihau? A hefyd, pa arian cyfred fyddai'n cael ei ddefnyddio? Ymddengys nad oes neb yn gwybod. Pwy sy'n talu'r ddyled honno? A beth sy'n digwydd i'r trosglwyddiadau cyllidol sy'n gweithredu ar hyn o bryd ledled y Deyrnas Unedig? Nid codi bwganod yw hyn; maent yn gwestiynau dilys am biliynau o bunnoedd o arian trethdalwyr.

Ond mae ein Teyrnas Unedig yn llawer mwy na mantolen yn unig. Edrychwch ar yr hanes, y soniwyd am beth ohono'n gynharach, ac a gynrychiolir gan deuluoedd ledled Cymru. Gwasanaethodd ein tadau, ein teidiau a'n hen-deidiau ochr yn ochr â dynion a menywod o Loegr, yr Alban a Gogledd Iwerddon trwy ddau ryfel byd. Ymladdodd catrodau Cymreig gyda dewrder eithriadol, dioddefodd cymunedau Cymru golled ac aberth, a ffarweliodd teuluoedd ag anwyliaid heb wybod a fyddent yn dychwelyd. Fe wnaethant wasanaethu'n rhan o luoedd arfog y Deyrnas Unedig, ac mae'r hanes cyffredin hwnnw'n bwysig.

Nid yw'n pennu pa benderfyniadau cyfansoddiadol y mae'n rhaid i genedlaethau'r dyfodol eu gwneud—ein penderfyniadau ni yw'r rheini—ond ni ddylem ddiystyru'r clymau a ffurfiwyd trwy genedlaethau o aberth cyffredin, ymdrechion cyffredin a chyflawniadau cyffredin. Mae'r clymau hynny'n parhau heddiw. Mae pobl yn croesi'r ffin rhwng Cymru a Lloegr bob dydd i weithio, masnachu, astudio, derbyn gofal iechyd ac ymweld â'u teuluoedd. Mae busnesau'n gweithredu ar ei thraws, mae cadwyni cyflenwi yn ei chroesi, teuluoedd yn ei chroesi. Rydym yn rhannu lluoedd arfog, rydym yn rhannu sefydliadau economaidd, rydym yn rhannu risgiau. Pan fydd angen cefnogaeth ar un rhan o'r Deyrnas Unedig, gall adnoddau symud rhwng ei chenhedloedd a'i rhanbarthau.

Gall Cymru barhau'n falch o'i Chymreigrwydd unigryw, gan barhau i fod yn rhan o rywbeth mwy o faint yn ogystal. Nid yw ein hiaith, ein diwylliant, ein cymunedau a'n hunaniaeth genedlaethol yn dibynnu ar godi ffin ryngwladol newydd. Pan gynigir annibyniaeth, rhaid i'r ddadl fynd y tu hwnt i apêl emosiynol mwy o sofraniaeth. Mae angen atebion credadwy ar y rhai sy'n cefnogi newid cyfansoddiadol sylfaenol ynglŷn â dyled, y diffyg cyllidol, pensiynau, arian, masnach, amddiffyn a chyllido gwasanaethau cyhoeddus. Mae'r ffigurau dan sylw'n rhy fawr a'r canlyniadau'n rhy bwysig i gael unrhyw beth llai na hynny. Rwy'n credu bod gan bob un ohonom yn y Siambr gyfrifoldeb i ddeall hanes ac etifeddiaeth y Deyrnas Unedig y gwnaeth cenedlaethau o'n blaenau ein helpu i'w hadeiladu, ei hamddiffyn a'i throsglwyddo ymlaen.

Dylem feddwl yn ofalus iawn cyn rhoi camau ymrannol ac anadferadwy o bosibl ar waith heb wynebu'r holl ganlyniadau i'r rhai a ddaw ar ein holau. O'm rhan i, rwy'n falch o fod yn Gymro, rwy'n falch o fod yn Brydeiniwr, a byddaf yn parhau i ddadlau'r achos dros ddiogelu ein lle yn y Deyrnas Unedig, nid yn unig oherwydd yr hanes a rannwn, ond oherwydd y dyfodol y mae gennym gyfle o hyd i'w adeiladu gyda'n gilydd. Diolch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Member_job_title_Welsh: Y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Effeithiolrwydd Llywodraeth a’r Cyfansoddiad
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch yn fawr iawn, Lywydd. A gaf i atgoffa pawb yn y Siambr hon bod hon yn ddadl sydd wedi'i alw gan Reform UK? Roedd Prif Weinidog Cymru ddoe yn siarad am iechyd, am ofal plant, am yr economi. Reform UK sy'n dewis canolbwyntio ar faterion cyfansoddiadol.

Ond mae gwelliant y Llywodraeth yn un syml—a dwi'n falch i glywed bod yna gefnogaeth iddo fe mewn mwy nag un plaid ar lawr y Siambr yma—sef y dylai pobl Cymru benderfynu ar ddyfodol cyfansoddiadol ein gwlad. Fel rŷn ni wedi'i glywed heddiw, mae gan Aelodau o'r Senedd hon farn wahanol am ble y dylai Cymru fod yn y pen draw yn gyfansoddiadol. Mae'r gwahaniaethau hynny yn gwbl ddilys mewn deddfwrfa ddemocrataidd. Ond dwi'n gobeithio y gallwn ni i gyd gytuno ar ddau beth: y dylai dyfodol Cymru gael ei benderfynu'n ddemocrataidd gan bobl Cymru, ac yn ail, y dylai Cymru gael y pwerau, yr adnoddau a'r offer sydd eu hangen i gyflawni dros bobl yma ac yn awr. Yr egwyddorion hyn sy'n sail i welliant y Llywodraeth heddiw. Dyw ein gwelliant ni ddim yn gofyn i Aelodau roi'r gorau i'w barn; mae'n gofyn i ni gydnabod egwyddor y gobeithiaf y gall ennyn cefnogaeth ar draws y Siambr, a dyw e ddim yn safbwynt pleidiol.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Thank you very much, Llywydd. May I remind everyone in this Chamber that this is a debate that has been called by Reform UK? The First Minister yesterday was talking about health, about childcare, about the economy. Reform UK has chosen to focus on constitutional issues.

But the Government's amendment is a simple one—and I'm pleased to hear that there is support for it from more than one party on the floor of this Chamber—which is that the people of Wales should determine the constitutional future of our country. As we have heard today, Members of this Senedd have different views about where Wales should be constitutionally, and those differences are completely valid in a democratic legislature. But I do hope that we can all agree on two things: that Wales's future should be determined democratically by the people of Wales, and secondly, that Wales should have the powers, the resources and the tools that it needs to deliver on behalf of people here and now. It is these principles that are the basis of the Government's amendment today. Our amendment doesn't ask Members to give up their views; it asks us to acknowledge a principle that hopefully will gain support from across the Chamber, and it is not a party political viewpoint.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
The principle is one that has been widely recognised.

'National aspirations must be respected; peoples may...be...governed only by their own consent.'

That was Woodrow Wilson to Congress in 1918. The self-determination of peoples is in the first article of the UN charter. Talking of our Scottish friends,

'as a nation, they have an undoubted right to national self-determination'.

I didn't expect myself to be quoting Baroness Thatcher approvingly in this Chamber, but she was right, of course—on that matter. [Interruption.] Wait for it. But we must put the people at the heart of constitutional change, because the UK is a 'voluntary nation of nations'—Gordon Brown, the former Prime Minister, in the commission on the UK's future. And yesterday, the Scottish Parliament agreed that

'the Parliament agrees that Scotland...has a right to decide its own future.'
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Mae'r egwyddor yn un sydd wedi cael ei chydnabod yn eang.

'Mae'n rhaid parchu dyheadau cenedlaethol; dim ond drwy eu cydsyniad eu hunain y dylid...llywodraethu...pobloedd.'

Woodrow Wilson a ddywedodd hynny wrth y Gyngres ym 1918. Mae hunanbenderfyniaeth pobloedd wedi'i gynnwys yn erthygl gyntaf siarter y Cenhedloedd Unedig. A sôn am ein ffrindiau Albanaidd,

'fel cenedl, mae ganddynt hawl ddiamau i hunanbenderfyniaeth cenedlaethol'.

Nid oeddwn yn disgwyl dyfynnu'r Farwnes Thatcher mewn ffordd gadarnhaol yn y Siambr hon, ond roedd hi'n llygad ei lle, wrth gwrs—ar y mater hwnnw. [Torri ar draws.] Un eiliad. Ond mae’n rhaid inni roi'r bobl wrth wraidd newid cyfansoddiadol, gan fod y DU yn 'genedl wirfoddol o genhedloedd'—Gordon Brown, cyn Brif Weinidog y DU, yn y comisiwn ar ddyfodol y DU. A ddoe, cytunodd Senedd yr Alban fod

'y Senedd yn cytuno bod gan yr Alban…hawl i benderfynu ei dyfodol ei hun.'

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl Reform UK: Cymru a'r Deyrnas Unedig
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Reform UK Debate: Wales and the United Kingdom
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Os oes un wers o'r chwarter canrif diwethaf o ddatganoli, dyma hi: dyw'r setliad cyfansoddiadol ddim yn sefyll yn ei hunfan. Mi ddywedodd rhywun rhywle fod datganoli yn broses, ddim yn ddigwyddiad. Nid y cwestiwn yw a fydd newid cyfansoddiadol yn digwydd; y cwestiwn yw sut y gallwn sicrhau bod Cymru yn barod ar gyfer y newid hwnnw, yn gallu dylanwadu arno ac yn elwa ohono. I'r Llywodraeth hon, mae hynny'n golygu diwygiadau ymarferol sy'n ein helpu ni i sicrhau canlyniadau gwell i bobl ar lawr gwlad ac i gymunedau. Nid mater damcaniaethol yn unig yw diwygio cyfansoddiadol; mae'n sicrhau bod gennym y pwerau, yr adnoddau a'r offer i gyflawni dros bobl Cymru.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: If there is one lesson to learn from the last quarter of a century of devolution, it is this: the constitutional settlement is not static. Someone somewhere said that devolution is a process, not an event. The question is not will constitutional change happen; the question is how can we ensure that Wales is ready for that change, can influence it and benefit from it. For this Government, that means practical changes that help us to ensure better results and outcomes for people on the ground and for communities. This is not a theoretical matter, that's not what constitutional change is; it is ensuring that we have the powers, the resources and the tools to deliver for the people of Wales.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl Reform UK: Cymru a'r Deyrnas Unedig
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Reform UK Debate: Wales and the United Kingdom
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
That's why our priorities in terms of devolution are clear. We made the case for progress on devolving rail infrastructure, on justice and policing, and on the Crown Estate. These are areas where there is substantial evidence, significant public interest and support that reaches well beyond a single political party. They will lead to a better train service, to lower energy bills, to safer communities—real changes to people's lives here in Wales. I've been heartened by the positive approach from the UK Government in response to those calls, and I hope we can conclude those discussions constructively.

Our objective isn't to move powers between institutions, but to ensure responsibilities sit at the level where they can be exercised most effectively and deliver the best outcomes for people and communities. And let me be clear to my colleagues here: it does indeed mean decentralisation within Wales as part of that package. We are decentralists in Plaid Cymru and we believe in those principles as a key area for us.

Turning to some of the points made in the debate, I do reflect there is a certain irony, particularly from colleagues opposite, in their support for the free movement of goods, capital, services and people, and of a large union that would bring all of those freedoms together. I would remind people that that was voted upon some years ago, and it remains our position that Wales would be better off in such a large European union.

There have also been points about the proud history of Wales, the proud history of Wales in the industrial revolution. And yet we have also heard from the benches opposite that that great nation that powered the industrial revolution—and we've heard of its great success—has fiscal challenges today. That is the legacy of the British state. We've heard about Slovenia, which saw a growth of 33 per cent in its gross domestic product in 10 years. We've heard about other countries who've seen growth far in excess of the Welsh context—successful independent countries—in this debate here.

But let's return to the fundamental point of our amendment and of this debate, in the view of the Government. Members here will disagree as to where Wales should ultimately be heading, but I do sincerely hope that we can agree on some basic fundamentals: that Wales's future should be determined democratically, and that change should be informed by evidence, not assertion. The public debate is stronger when it includes a wide range of voices and perspectives, and it is our shared responsibility to ensure that Wales has the confidence, the capacity and the tools to shape its own future. The people of Wales, Llywydd, are sovereign. It is for us to determine our future, wherever that may lead us. Diolch yn fawr.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Dyna pam y mae ein blaenoriaethau mewn perthynas â datganoli'n glir. Fe wnaethom ddadlau'r achos dros gynnydd ar ddatganoli seilwaith rheilffyrdd, ar gyfiawnder a phlismona, ac ar Ystad y Goron. Dyma feysydd lle mae tystiolaeth sylweddol, diddordeb cyhoeddus sylweddol a chefnogaeth sy'n ymestyn ymhell y tu hwnt i un blaid wleidyddol. Byddant yn arwain at wasanaethau trên gwell, at filiau ynni is, at gymunedau mwy diogel—newidiadau go iawn i fywydau pobl yma yng Nghymru. Cefais fy nghalonogi gan yr ymagwedd gadarnhaol gan Lywodraeth y DU mewn ymateb i'r galwadau hynny, ac rwy'n gobeithio y gallwn gwblhau'r trafodaethau hynny'n adeiladol.

Nid symud pwerau rhwng sefydliadau yw ein nod, ond sicrhau bod cyfrifoldebau'n bodoli ar y lefel lle gellir eu harfer yn fwyaf effeithiol a lle gellir cyflawni'r canlyniadau gorau i bobl a chymunedau. A gadewch imi ddweud yn glir wrth fy nghyd-Aelodau yma: mae'n golygu, yn wir, datganoli o fewn Cymru fel rhan o'r pecyn hwnnw. Rydym yn ddatganolwyr ym Mhlaid Cymru, ac rydym yn credu yn yr egwyddorion hynny fel maes allweddol i ni.

Gan droi at rai o'r pwyntiau a wnaed yn y ddadl, credaf fod rhywfaint o eironi, yn enwedig gan ein cyd-Aelodau gyferbyn, yn eu cefnogaeth i symudiad rhydd nwyddau, cyfalaf, gwasanaethau a phobl, ac i undeb mawr a fyddai'n dod â'r holl ryddid hwnnw ynghyd. Hoffwn atgoffa pobl y cafwyd pleidlais ar hynny rai blynyddoedd yn ôl, ac rydym yn parhau i fod o'r farn y byddai Cymru mewn gwell sefyllfa mewn undeb Ewropeaidd mawr o'r fath.

Gwnaed pwyntiau hefyd am hanes balch Cymru, hanes balch Cymru yn y chwyldro diwydiannol. Ac eto, rydym hefyd wedi clywed gan y meinciau gyferbyn fod y genedl wych honno a bwerodd y chwyldro diwydiannol—ac rydym wedi clywed am ei llwyddiant mawr—yn wynebu heriau ariannol heddiw. Dyna etifeddiaeth y wladwriaeth Brydeinig. Rydym wedi clywed am Slofenia, a welodd dwf o 33 y cant yn ei chynnyrch domestig gros mewn 10 mlynedd. Rydym wedi clywed am wledydd eraill sydd wedi gweld twf ymhell y tu hwnt i'r cyd-destun Cymreig—gwledydd annibynnol llwyddiannus—yn y ddadl hon yma.

Ond gadewch inni ddychwelyd at bwynt sylfaenol ein gwelliant a'r ddadl hon, ym marn y Llywodraeth. Bydd yr Aelodau yma'n anghytuno ynghylch ble y dylai Cymru anelu yn y pen draw, ond rwy'n mawr obeithio y gallwn gytuno ar rai pethau sylfaenol: y dylid penderfynu ar ddyfodol Cymru yn ddemocrataidd, ac y dylai newid gael ei lywio gan dystiolaeth, nid haeriadau. Mae'r ddadl gyhoeddus yn gryfach pan fydd yn cynnwys ystod eang o leisiau a safbwyntiau, a'n cyfrifoldeb ni ar y cyd yw sicrhau bod gan Gymru hyder, gallu a dulliau gweithredu i lunio'i dyfodol ei hun. Mae pobl Cymru, Lywydd, yn sofran. Ein lle ni yw penderfynu ein dyfodol, lle bynnag y gall hynny ein harwain. Diolch yn fawr.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 7. Dadl Reform UK: Cymru a'r Deyrnas Unedig
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Reform UK Debate: Wales and the United Kingdom
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch, Llywydd. Can I thank everybody contributing to such a lively debate this afternoon? There's nothing more I love in this Chamber than talking about the second greatest union in my life—other than my marriage, of course—and that is the great union of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and the great benefits that it brings to the people right the way across these islands.

We opened with Adrian. As you said, we are Welsh, but we are also British. We can be both, and far too often this debate gets polarised between the two. And as we've seen during the election, Plaid Cymru like to politicise Welshness, which is an absolute disgrace. You also raised the point about the United Kingdom being our biggest trading partner. We know that. We know how important the United Kingdom is to us. But what would Plaid Cymru want us to do? They'd want to make us poorer and more reliant on the state, something that we all fundamentally disagree with.

You also raised an important point about defence. That's something that keeps us safe at night. It keeps us safe in our beds, and that is something we should always be proud of. Because, as Darren Millar raised, those are questions that Plaid Cymru simply cannot answer when they're asked about it. They dodge the question because they know they do not know the answer. You did raise the constitutional arrangements of these islands. Yes, they're not perfect, but what is the alternative? Who would we see as a President of Wales? Maybe the ex-Llywydd and Minister may be a candidate, who knows? But I don't think we need to change the arrangements that we currently have. Because Plaid would hold us at the back of the queue, and I think the Minister summed this up. They want to join the EU, but they want to leave another union. The hypocrisy in their argument is absolutely astounding.

I agree with Huw from Labour. I agree with you on the point that Wales is stronger within the United Kingdom. That is something that we on these benches share with you—that we are stronger together. You said you weren't a member of Plaid Cymru, but by recent events, there is still time. So, just bear with yourself, you never know what could happen. They'll take anybody at the minute.

You also talked about the £7,000, about people being poorer. That is something we have to be clear about. The IFS have been very clear on this: that Wales would be poorer if we were an independent nation. But you also talked about wanting to devolve powers down to local government. The irony in that is you had 27 years to do that, and all Labour were interested in was 27 years of centralisation here in this building. So, I don't know when the change is coming. Maybe new leader Ken Skates has different views. That wasn't the view of some of the extreme socialists who were there before.

And then we had Carrie Harper. You talked about managed decline. I would just gently say to you that the reason why Wales has had managed decline is because you've propped up previous Welsh Labour Governments for years and years. If there's anyone who's managed decline—. It's not the fault of the United Kingdom, it's the fault of yourselves for propping up Welsh Labour over the years.

Gareth, you talked about the First Minister perhaps misleading the public—I can't say the word I said the other day, or the Llywydd will pull me up again—the simple reason being that we were told that independence was not on the ballot paper. This wasn't going to be discussed. But what do we see at the first opportunity? The First Minister is quite happy to stand with the socialist cabal and the separatist cabal who are keen to rip apart our United Kingdom and talk with people who sponsored state terrorism against our country—an absolute disgrace. And you also talked about the Government needing to get on with the day job. How much Government time and money and energy is being wasted on this, looking at Welsh independence, when we have a pro-union majority in this Senedd? I think the Government need to remember that.

Darren Millar, I really enjoyed your contribution. I didn't think we could ever get Mystic Meg into a contribution. [Laughter.] I'm not quite sure she'd be happy about the arrangement. You talked about our shared history, the blood, sweat and tears to protect, build and defend these islands. And you also talked about our armed forces, as others did. But as you said, Plaid can't answer the questions on the future. How are we going to sort out our policing? How are we going to sort out our defence? How are we going to sort out social security? Plaid have no answer for that. They're selling a pipe dream to people. And as we've seen through all the polls, the Welsh public are not buying it.

Elfed, you said that people in Wales didn't want Labour. And I agree, they didn't want Labour, but they didn't want independence either. What you see in this Chamber is a majority, and people voted in their droves for parties who are pro-union. They even voted for the Lib Dems, who've switched their position to pro-union now as well. Because we want to make sure we are stronger within the United Kingdom. I'm afraid I didn't agree with much else that you said.

Francesca O'Brien—a very passionate speech. You highlighted that the United Kingdom is the best country in this world, and I think everybody in this Chamber should agree with that. We should not be ashamed of our shared history. We should not be ashamed of our world history either. Britain built the world. You talked about how Welsh people have shaped our globe, how we have improved democracy, how we have brought freedoms to people around the globe. And I'm afraid to say what we see in this Chamber—[Interruption.] What we see in this Chamber, Llywydd, is political opportunism by others, rewriting our history to suit a political narrative to rip our country apart.

Mike Hedges—I always like your contributions, Mike, because you speak with a lot of experience about the Welsh tax receipts, about GVA, and Wales just not being able to afford our public services across this country if we become an independent nation. That is a matter of fact. But it's something yet again Plaid can't talk about. And also, the Institute for Fiscal Studies's report—that has always been very clear that Wales would not be able to afford to be an independent nation.

And Iain McIntosh, you raised a lot of points, as others, but you said that that shared history that we have across this country is very, very important.

Then we come to the First Minister's human shield, Dafydd Trystan Davies, who seems to be rolled out all the time to deal with things that the First Minister doesn't want to deal with, because he's too busy making a TikTok video somewhere, I suspect. [Interruption.] Yes, I will conclude after this. And you talked about the future of our nation. We want a strong Wales in a strong United Kingdom, because we believe that the people of Wales deserve to be part of our United Kingdom. We have helped to build it. We help to maintain it. And on these benches, we will always support it.

So, if Members across this Chamber want to support our union for a safer, stronger future across our United Kingdom, support our motion, reject the amendments and vote with us today.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Diolch, Lywydd. A gaf i ddiolch i bawb sydd wedi cyfrannu at ddadl mor fywiog y prynhawn yma? Nid oes unrhyw beth rwy'n fwy hoff ohono yn y Siambr hon na siarad am yr ail undeb gorau yn fy mywyd—ar ôl fy mhriodas, wrth gwrs—sef undeb gwych Teyrnas Unedig Prydain Fawr a Gogledd Iwerddon, a'r manteision mawr y mae'n eu dwyn i'r bobl ar draws yr ynysoedd hyn.

Fe wnaethom agor gydag Adrian. Fel y dywedoch chi, rydym yn Gymry, ond rydym hefyd yn Brydeinwyr. Gallwn fod y ddau beth, ac yn rhy aml, mae'r ddadl hon yn pegynu rhwng y ddau beth. Ac fel y gwelsom yn yr etholiad, mae Plaid Cymru yn hoffi gwleidyddoli Cymreictod, sy'n gwbl warthus. Fe godoch chi'r pwynt hefyd ynglŷn â'r Deyrnas Unedig fel ein partner masnachu mwyaf. Rydym yn gwybod hynny. Rydym yn gwybod pa mor bwysig yw'r Deyrnas Unedig i ni. Ond beth fyddai Plaid Cymru eisiau i ni ei wneud? Byddent eisiau ein gwneud yn dlotach ac yn fwy dibynnol ar y wladwriaeth, rhywbeth y mae pob un ohonom yn anghytuno'n llwyr yn ei gylch.

Fe godoch chi bwynt pwysig hefyd ynglŷn ag amddiffyn. Mae hynny'n rhywbeth sy'n ein cadw'n ddiogel yn y nos. Mae'n ein cadw'n ddiogel yn ein gwelyau, ac mae hynny'n rhywbeth y dylem fod yn falch ohono bob amser. Oherwydd, fel y nododd Darren Millar, mae'r rheini'n gwestiynau na all Plaid Cymru mo'u hateb pan gânt eu gofyn iddynt. Maent yn osgoi'r cwestiwn am eu bod yn gwybod nad ydynt yn gwybod yr ateb. Fe godoch chi drefniadau cyfansoddiadol yr ynysoedd hyn. Iawn, nid ydynt yn berffaith, ond beth yw'r dewis arall? Pwy fyddem yn eu gweld fel Arlywydd Cymru? Efallai y byddai'r cyn-Lywydd a'r Gweinidog yn ymgeiswyr, pwy a ŵyr? Ond ni chredaf fod angen inni newid y trefniadau sydd gennym ar hyn o bryd. Oherwydd byddai Plaid Cymru yn ein dal yng nghefn y ciw, a chredaf fod y Gweinidog wedi crynhoi hyn. Maent eisiau ymuno â'r UE, ond maent eisiau gadael undeb arall. Mae'r rhagrith yn eu dadl yn gwbl syfrdanol.

Rwy'n cytuno â Huw o'r Blaid Lafur. Rwy'n cytuno â chi ynglŷn â'r pwynt fod Cymru'n gryfach o fewn y Deyrnas Unedig. Mae hynny'n rhywbeth rydym ni ar y meinciau hyn yn ei rannu gyda chi—ein bod yn gryfach gyda'n gilydd. Fe ddywedoch chi nad oeddech yn aelod o Blaid Cymru, ond o ystyried digwyddiadau diweddar, mae amser o hyd. Felly, byddwch yn amyneddgar, ni wyddoch beth all ddigwydd. Maent yn derbyn unrhyw un ar hyn o bryd.

Fe sonioch chi hefyd am y £7,000, y bydd pobl yn dlotach. Mae hynny'n rhywbeth y mae'n rhaid inni fod yn glir yn ei gylch. Mae'r Sefydliad Astudiaethau Cyllidol wedi dweud hyn yn glir iawn: y byddai Cymru'n dlotach pe baem yn genedl annibynnol. Ond fe sonioch chi hefyd am fod eisiau datganoli pwerau i lywodraeth leol. Yr eironi yn hynny o beth yw eich bod wedi cael 27 mlynedd i wneud hynny, a'r cyfan roedd gan Lafur ddiddordeb ynddo oedd 27 mlynedd o ganoli yma yn yr adeilad hwn. Felly, nid wyf yn gwybod pryd y mae'r newid yn dod. Efallai fod gan yr arweinydd newydd Ken Skates safbwyntiau gwahanol. Nid dyna oedd barn rhai o'r sosialwyr eithafol a oedd yno'n flaenorol.

Ac yna cawsom Carrie Harper. Fe sonioch chi am ddirywiad wedi'i reoli. Buaswn yn dweud yn garedig wrthych mai'r rheswm pam y mae Cymru wedi cael dirywiad wedi'i reoli yw am eich bod wedi cynnal Llywodraethau Llafur blaenorol Cymru am flynyddoedd maith. Os oes unrhyw un sydd wedi rheoli dirywiad—. Nid bai'r Deyrnas Unedig yw hyn, ond eich bai chi'ch hunain am gynnal Llafur Cymru dros y blynyddoedd.

Gareth, fe sonioch chi am y Prif Weinidog efallai’n camarwain y cyhoedd—ni allaf ddweud y gair a ddywedais y diwrnod o’r blaen, neu bydd y Llywydd yn fy ngheryddu eto—y rheswm syml yw eu bod wedi dweud wrthym nad oedd annibyniaeth ar y papur pleidleisio. Nid oedd yn mynd i gael ei drafod. Ond beth a welwn ar y cyfle cyntaf? Mae’r Prif Weinidog yn fwy na pharod i gyd-sefyll gyda’r cabál o sosialwyr a’r cabál o ymwahanwr sydd eisiau rhwygo ein Teyrnas Unedig yn ddarnau a siarad â phobl a ariannodd derfysgaeth wladwriaethol yn erbyn ein gwlad—hollol warthus. Ac fe sonioch chi hefyd am yr angen i’r Llywodraeth fwrw ymlaen â’r gwaith o ddydd i ddydd. Faint o amser ac arian ac egni’r Llywodraeth sy’n cael ei wastraffu ar hyn, ar edrych ar annibyniaeth Cymru, pan fo gennym fwyafrif o blaid yr undeb yn y Senedd hon? Rwy'n credu bod angen i’r Llywodraeth gofio hynny.

Darren Millar, mwynheais eich cyfraniad yn fawr iawn. Ni feddyliais y byddem yn cael cyfeiriad at Mystic Meg mewn cyfraniad. [Chwerthin.] Nid wyf yn siŵr a fyddai'n fodlon iawn ar y trefniant. Fe sonioch chi am ein hanes cyffredin, y gwaed, y chwys a'r dagrau a gollwyd er mwyn diogelu, adeiladu ac amddiffyn yr ynysoedd hyn. Ac fe sonioch chi hefyd am ein lluoedd arfog, fel y gwnaeth eraill. Ond fel y dywedoch chi, ni all Plaid Cymru ateb y cwestiynau ynglŷn â'r dyfodol. Beth a wnawn ynghylch plismona? Beth a wnawn ynghylch amddiffyn? Beth a wnawn ynghylch nawdd cymdeithasol? Nid oes gan Blaid Cymru ateb i hynny. Maent yn gwerthu breuddwyd gwrach i bobl. Ac fel y gwelsom drwy'r holl arolygon barn, nid yw'r cyhoedd yng Nghymru eisiau hynny.

Elfed, fe ddywedoch chi nad oedd pobl Cymru eisiau Llafur. Ac rwy'n cytuno, nid oeddent eisiau Llafur, ond nid oeddent eisiau annibyniaeth chwaith. Yr hyn a welwch yn y Siambr hon yw mwyafrif, a phleidleisiodd pobl yn eu lluoedd dros bleidiau sydd o blaid yr undeb. Fe wnaethant bleidleisio dros y Democratiaid Rhyddfrydol hyd yn oed, sydd wedi newid eu safbwynt i fod o blaid yr undeb nawr hefyd. Oherwydd rydym eisiau sicrhau ein bod yn gryfach o fewn y Deyrnas Unedig. Mae arnaf ofn nad oeddwn yn cytuno â fawr ddim arall a ddywedoch chi.

Francesca O'Brien—araith angerddol iawn. Fe nodoch chi'r ffaith mai'r Deyrnas Unedig yw'r wlad orau yn y byd, ac rwy'n credu y dylai pawb yn y Siambr gytuno â hynny. Ni ddylem fod â chywilydd am ein hanes cyffredin. Ni ddylem fod â chywilydd am ein hanes yn fyd-eang chwaith. Prydain a adeiladodd y byd. Fe sonioch chi sut y mae pobl Cymru wedi llunio ein byd, sut rydym wedi gwella democratiaeth, sut rydym wedi dod â rhyddid i bobl ym mhob cwr o'r byd. Ac mae arnaf ofn mai'r hyn a welwn yn y Siambr hon—[Torri ar draws.] Yr hyn a welwn yn y Siambr hon, Lywydd, yw oportiwnistiaeth wleidyddol gan eraill, sy'n ailysgrifennu ein hanes i gyd-fynd â naratif gwleidyddol i rwygo ein gwlad yn ddarnau.

Mike Hedges—rwyf bob amser yn hoff o'ch cyfraniadau, Mike, gan eich bod yn siarad gyda llawer o brofiad am dderbyniadau treth Cymru, am werth ychwanegol gros, a'r ffaith na fyddai Cymru'n gallu fforddio ein gwasanaethau cyhoeddus ledled y wlad hon pe byddem yn dod yn genedl annibynnol. Mae hynny’n ffaith. Ond mae’n rhywbeth na all Plaid Cymru siarad amdano unwaith eto. A hefyd, adroddiad y Sefydliad Astudiaethau Cyllidol—mae hwnnw bob amser wedi dweud yn glir iawn na fyddai Cymru’n gallu fforddio bod yn genedl annibynnol.

Ac Iain McIntosh, fe godoch chi lawer o bwyntiau, fel y gwnaeth eraill, ond fe ddywedoch chi fod yr hanes cyffredin sydd gennym ar draws y wlad hon yn bwysig iawn.

Yna, down at darian ddynol y Prif Weinidog, Dafydd Trystan Davies, sydd fel pe bai'n cael ei ddefnyddio drwy'r amser i ddelio â phethau nad yw'r Prif Weinidog eisiau delio â nhw, am ei fod yn rhy brysur yn gwneud fideo TikTok yn rhywle, rwy'n tybio. [Torri ar draws.] Iawn, fe wnaf ddirwyn i ben ar ôl hyn. Ac fe sonioch chi am ddyfodol ein cenedl. Rydym ni eisiau Cymru gref mewn Teyrnas Unedig gref, am ein bod yn credu bod pobl Cymru yn haeddu bod yn rhan o'n Teyrnas Unedig. Rydym wedi helpu i'w hadeiladu. Rydym yn helpu i'w chynnal. Ac ar y meinciau hyn, byddwn bob amser yn ei chefnogi.

Felly, os yw Aelodau ar draws y Siambr hon eisiau cefnogi ein hundeb er mwyn sicrhau dyfodol mwy diogel a chryfach ar draws ein Teyrnas Unedig, cefnogwch ein cynnig, gwrthodwch y gwelliannau a phleidleisiwch gyda ni heddiw.
